title: Unit 10 — Career Opportunities
notes:
## 1. Topic Introduction — Writing Your Way Into a Future

Career is the theme where English stops being a subject and becomes a tool: the CV, the application letter, the interview answer and the LinkedIn summary are all language tasks with real consequences. This unit builds the vocabulary of work and ambition, the honest concepts behind choosing a career (passion, aptitude, market, luck — and their weights), and the practical writing genres NEB tests — job applications, CVs and the career essay — where layout and register earn marks as surely as ideas.

## 2. Fundamental Conceptual Understanding — How People Actually Choose Careers

### 2.1 Vocabulary architecture of the theme

- **Work words:** occupation, profession, vocation, career path, qualification, vacancy, recruit, internship, apprenticeship, promotion, resign, retire, freelance, entrepreneur.
- **Application words:** curriculum vitae (CV), resume, cover letter, reference, portfolio, shortlist, interview panel, job description, salary, perks, probation.
- **Modern shifts:** remote work, gig economy, upskilling, reskilling, portfolio career, work-life balance, burnout.

### 2.2 The four factors of a career choice — and their honest weights

**Interest** (what you can do for years without forcing yourself), **aptitude** (what you are actually good at — often different from interest), **opportunity** (what the market pays for, locally and abroad) and **values** (what you want your work to serve). Popular advice over-weights passion; the exam-worthy position balances all four: passion sustains effort, aptitude sets the ceiling, opportunity pays the bills, values decide whether success feels like success.

### 2.3 The Nepali career reality

Two forces dominate: the **abroad option** (labour migration and study-abroad drain talent, yet remittances sustain families — the choice is economic before it is romantic) and the **credential race** (degrees as tickets, entrance-exam economies, tuition everywhere). The mature essay treats migration as a symptom of the job market, and "brain drain" as a question — what would make staying rational?

### 2.4 The future of work, stated calmly

Automation removes routine tasks faster than routine people; the durable skills are judgement, communication, care and continuous learning. The honest conclusion is not "learn to code" but "**expect to retrain**" — careers are becoming sequences of skills, not single titles. Portability of skills is the new job security.

## 3. The Application Genres — Layout Is Marks

### 3.1 The CV: one page of evidence

Structure: name and contact → a two-line objective or profile (only if specific) → education (most recent first) → experience with **action verbs and results** ("organised a 12-team science fair", not "was responsible for events") → skills (languages, tools) → references ("available on request" is acceptable). No photo unless asked, no "father's name" in modern formats, no spelling errors anywhere — a CV with a typo is a self-disqualifying document.

### 3.2 The application letter: four paragraphs, no biography

(1) **Position and source** — "I wish to apply for the post of … advertised in … on …". (2) **Why you fit** — two proof points matched to the job description, not a life story. (3) **Enclosed CV** and availability for interview. (4) **Polite close** — "Yours faithfully/sincerely" (faithfully when you begin "Dear Sir/Madam", sincerely when you name the reader). Formal register throughout: no contractions, no "I am writing to you because I really really want…".

### 3.3 The interview answer: STAR in miniature

For "tell us about a challenge", the shape is **Situation** (one sentence), **Task** (what you had to do), **Action** (what you did — the longest part), **Result** (what changed, with a number if honest). Practice one academic and one personal STAR story before any interview; improvised answers circle, structured ones land.

## 4. Arguing About Careers — Frames That Fit the Questions

### 4.1 "Follow your passion" — the balanced verdict

For: passion funds the 10,000 hours mastery demands. Against: passion is often discovered *inside* competence, not before it — and the market must want what you love. Synthesis: follow **capability and curiosity**; passion tends to arrive as a passenger, not a driver.

### 4.2 "Brain drain: should Nepal worry?"

Concede the individual's right — a nurse in the UK earns in a month what she would in a year here. Rebut the nation's loss: training investment walks away. Then the synthesis examiners reward: remittances are the fee the country pays for not building the jobs; the fix is opportunity, not guilt — and the diaspora can be an asset (skills, networks, returnees) rather than only a leak.

### 4.3 "Vocational education versus university" — the false ranking

The question assumes a ladder with university on top. Rebut with the trades' economics: licensed electricians and plumbers out-earn many degree-holders and cannot be outsourced to a website. The honest claim is not "vocational is better" but "**the match** matters": aptitude to path, path to market. Dignity of labour is the paragraph's close, not its opening.

## 5. Master Comparison — Job versus Career versus Calling (the NEB classic)

| Basis | Job | Career | Calling |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Time horizon | this month | years, a trajectory | a life's work |
| Main motive | pay | advancement, mastery | meaning and service |
| Identity | "it's what I do" | "it's what I am" | "it's what I am for" |
| Effort pattern | minimum required | invested, strategic | self-renewing |
| Risk | stagnation | burnout, tunnel vision | exploitation of devotion |
| Financial reality | survives | builds | must still pay bills |
| Best relationship to the others | a start | the ladder | the compass |
| Exam use | define | narrate | argue the ideal |

## 6. Conceptual Relationships

- **Unit 1 → here:** "Do what you love" is a claim with an assumption (that love precedes competence) worth testing before you sign it.
- **Here → Unit 5 (education):** the credential race and the tuition economy are education's career shadow.
- **Here → Unit 6 (money):** salary negotiation, remittance economics and the gig economy link the two themes.
- **Here → writing units:** the application letter and CV are formal-writing genres; the career essay is the argument frame in personal dress.

## 7. Exam Orientation and Previous Year Questions (NEB)

### 7.1 The recurring question patterns

1. **Application letter with CV (8–10 marks):** an advertised post given in the question — layout first (this is where the marks live), four-paragraph letter, one-page CV with action verbs.
2. **Essay (8–10 marks):** "My aim in life" / "Brain drain" — personal aim essays need a reason ladder (why this field, what it serves, what you will do in it), not a diary.
3. **Short answers (2–4 marks):** "Distinguish a job from a career" — the §5 pair in one sentence each.
4. **Dialogue (4–6 marks):** career counselling between teacher and student — advice modals (*should, could, might want to*), two concrete options, no forced ending.

### 7.2 A worked miniature (application middle paragraph)

"My two years editing the college science magazine taught me exactly what the advertisement asks for: I planned a six-issue calendar, managed a team of nine writers and grew subscriptions from 120 to 310. I can bring the same discipline of deadlines and clarity of language to your communications team." — evidence with numbers, matched to the job, in two sentences.

### 7.3 Time strategy

For application tasks, spend the first three minutes copying the job's own key words into your margin — the letter must echo the advertisement's needs, not your autobiography. Proofread names and dates last; an error in the company's name is the fastest rejection ever written.
examShortTricks: Trick 1: Career questions test FORMAL WRITING: cover letter and CV conventions — follow the fixed format; content must match the advertised post.
Trick 2: Interview answers use the STAR frame: Situation, Task, Action, Result — one compact STAR example beats vague claims.
practiceQuestions: Q. Write a cover letter for a teaching vacancy. (4 marks) — format, post and source, two matching qualifications, availability.
Q. How should you answer 'tell me about yourself' in an interview? (2 marks) — brief education, relevant skills, one achievement — under a minute.
